samples.title: What Vibe Coding Is: Promise, Workflow and Risks
samples.definition: Vibe coding is a style of building software where you describe what you want in natural language and let an AI assistant write most of the code, judging progress mainly by whether the result runs and looks right. The term was popularised by Andrej Karpathy in early 2025. In professional settings it is a starting point: engineers still own the code, so they read, test and review what the AI produces before it ships.
objectives: Define vibe coding and distinguish it from disciplined AI-assisted engineering.
Describe the basic loop: describe, generate, run, inspect, refine.
Explain where vibe coding shines (prototypes, glue code) and where it is dangerous (auth, payments, data).
List the main risks of accepting code you have not read: bugs, security holes, licence and maintenance debt.
Answer interview questions about your personal policy for using AI-generated code.

interview.question: What is vibe coding?
interview.answer: It is building software by describing what you want in natural language and letting an AI assistant generate most of the code, iterating based on whether the result works, rather than writing and reasoning about every line yourself.
interview.explanation: A strong answer adds that it is great for speed and prototypes, and that professional use adds review and testing on top.

interview.question: How do you use AI coding tools in your own work?
interview.answer: I use them for scaffolding, boilerplate, exploring unfamiliar APIs and drafting tests. I keep changes small, read every diff, run tests and ask the assistant to explain code I do not understand. For security-sensitive code I review line by line.
interview.explanation: Interviewers want evidence of judgement. Mention concrete practices (small diffs, tests, review) rather than just 'I use Copilot'.

interview.question: What are the main risks of shipping AI-generated code without review?
interview.answer: Hidden bugs and missed edge cases, security flaws such as injection or missing authorisation, hallucinated or outdated APIs and packages, leaked secrets, and code nobody on the team understands well enough to maintain.
interview.explanation: Group risks into correctness, security, supply chain and maintainability; that structure signals senior thinking.

interview.question: When would you deliberately choose a fast vibe-coding approach?
interview.answer: For a prototype to validate an idea, a one-off script, or a demo where speed matters more than long-term quality, as long as it is clearly labelled and not deployed with real user data.
interview.explanation: Showing you can match rigour to risk is better than saying 'never' or 'always'.

interview.question: A teammate merged a large AI-generated pull request that 'works'. What would you check?
interview.answer: Whether there are tests and they pass, input validation and authorisation on any endpoints, secrets in code or config, new dependencies and their legitimacy, error handling, and whether the change can be split into smaller reviewable parts.
interview.explanation: This scenario tests review habits. Prioritise by risk and suggest process improvements such as size limits on AI-generated PRs.

example.title: A prototype that works but is not production-ready
example.body: A student asks an assistant: 'Build a page where users sign up with email and password and see a dashboard.' Within minutes the page works in the browser. A review then finds that passwords are stored in plain text in localStorage, there is no server-side check, and the dashboard is visible to anyone who edits a flag in the browser. The demo is fine for a hackathon; shipping it would be a security incident. The fix is to move authentication to a server, hash passwords and check sessions on every request.

practice.title: Triage AI-generated changes by risk
practice.statement: A team receives several AI-generated changes. Each change has a name, a number of changed lines, an area and whether it includes tests. Score each change: area weight ui=1, logic=2, data=3, auth=4, payments=4 (any other area counts as 2). Add 2 if more than 400 lines changed, otherwise add 1 if more than 100 lines changed. Add 2 if the change has no tests. A score of 6 or more is HIGH, 4 or 5 is MEDIUM, anything lower is LOW. Print each change's level, then the change to review first (highest score; on a tie, the earliest one).
practice.objective: Turn the idea 'scale review effort with risk' into a simple, explicit scoring rule.

takeaways: Vibe coding means describing intent and letting AI write the code, judging by results.
The core loop is describe, generate, run, inspect and refine.
It is ideal for prototypes and low-risk code, risky for auth, payments and data.
Plausible code is not proven code: read diffs and run tests.
You own every line you merge, regardless of who or what wrote it.
Scale the amount of review with the cost of a bug.

samples.title: How AI Coding Assistants Work: Tokens, Context and Prediction
samples.definition: An AI coding assistant is an application built on a large language model (LLM), a neural network trained on huge amounts of text and code to predict the next token given the tokens before it. The assistant collects relevant context (your prompt, open files, project rules, search results), sends it to the model, and turns the predicted tokens into suggestions, chat answers or file edits. The model has no live view of your project beyond what fits in that context.
objectives: Explain that a large language model generates code by predicting the next token.
Describe tokens, the context window and why context size limits what the model can 'see'.
Explain how assistants build context from open files, search results and instructions.
Relate temperature and training cut-off to non-determinism and outdated APIs.
Choose which files to give an assistant when the context budget is limited.

interview.question: How does an LLM generate code?
interview.answer: It predicts the next token from the tokens before it, appends the chosen token and repeats until it finishes. It learned which continuations are likely from training on large amounts of code and text.
interview.explanation: Mention that it optimises for likelihood, not correctness; that explains hallucinated APIs.

interview.question: What is a context window and why does it matter for coding assistants?
interview.answer: It is the maximum number of tokens the model can process in one request, including the prompt, files and the answer. Code outside the window is invisible to the model, so it may duplicate helpers or ignore conventions it cannot see.
interview.explanation: Strong answers connect context limits to practical behaviour such as forgetting instructions in long chats.

interview.question: Why does the same prompt sometimes give different code?
interview.answer: Models sample tokens from a probability distribution, and settings such as temperature add variation. Context differences between runs also change the result.
interview.explanation: Add that this is why you verify with tests rather than expecting identical output.

interview.question: Why might an assistant suggest a deprecated API, and how do you prevent it?
interview.answer: Its knowledge stops at its training cut-off and older usage is often more common in training data. Specify versions, paste current documentation or let an agent read the docs, and verify by running the code.
interview.explanation: Naming a concrete mitigation such as pinning versions in the prompt shows practical experience.

interview.question: What makes an agentic coding assistant different from autocomplete?
interview.answer: An agent runs the model in a loop with tools: it can read and edit files, run commands and tests, observe results and decide the next step. Autocomplete only predicts text at the cursor.
interview.explanation: Mention the extra responsibility: sandboxing, permission prompts and reviewing the final diff.

example.title: Why the assistant invented a helper
example.body: A developer asks an assistant in a fresh chat to 'add a function to format prices like the rest of the app'. The model has not seen the existing formatPrice helper in utils/money.js, so it writes a new one using toFixed(2) and the dollar sign. After the developer attaches utils/money.js, the assistant reuses formatPrice and the rupee format. The model was not 'wrong'; it lacked context.

practice.title: Pack files into a context budget
practice.statement: You have a token budget and a list of files. Estimate each file's tokens as ceil(chars / 4). Consider files in order of priority (1 is most important); files with equal priority keep their input order. Include a file if it fits in the remaining budget, otherwise skip it and continue with the next file. Print the included files, the skipped files and the tokens used.
practice.objective: Practise choosing context for an assistant when the token budget is limited.

takeaways: LLMs generate code token by token by predicting likely continuations.
The context window limits what the model can see; outside it, information does not exist.
Assistants build context from cursor code, retrieval, project rules and tool output.
Sampling makes output vary between runs; tests make results trustworthy.
Training cut-offs cause outdated API suggestions; supply current docs when it matters.
Relevant, focused context improves output more than long, noisy context.

samples.title: HTML Semantics and Document Structure
samples.definition: Semantic HTML means choosing elements for what content is, not how it looks: a navigation menu goes in nav, the primary content in main, a clickable action in button, and section titles in h1–h6. Browsers, search engines and assistive technologies such as screen readers use these meanings to understand and navigate the page. Styling is applied separately with CSS.
objectives: Explain what semantic HTML is and why it matters for accessibility, SEO and maintenance.
Use landmark elements (header, nav, main, article, section, aside, footer) correctly.
Build a logical heading hierarchy and connect form inputs to labels.
Spot 'div soup' and non-semantic patterns in AI-generated markup.
Write a program that checks a heading outline for skipped levels.

interview.question: What is semantic HTML?
interview.answer: Using HTML elements according to the meaning of the content, such as nav for navigation, button for actions and h1–h6 for headings, rather than generic divs and spans styled to look right.
interview.explanation: Add the benefits: accessibility, SEO and readable code.

interview.question: What is the difference between section, article and div?
interview.answer: article is self-contained content that makes sense on its own, like a post or a product card. section groups thematically related content, normally with a heading. div has no meaning and is used for layout or styling hooks when nothing else fits.
interview.explanation: Interviewers like the 'could it be syndicated on its own?' test for article.

interview.question: Why is <div onclick> a bad substitute for <button>?
interview.answer: A div is not focusable by keyboard, does not respond to Enter or Space, and is not announced as a button by screen readers. Recreating that needs tabindex, a role and key handlers, while <button> provides it all natively.
interview.explanation: This is the most common accessibility flaw in generated UIs, so mention you check for it in reviews.

interview.question: How should headings be structured on a page?
interview.answer: One h1 that describes the page, then h2 for main sections, h3 for subsections and so on, without skipping levels when going deeper. Levels reflect structure; visual size is controlled by CSS.
interview.explanation: Mention that screen reader users navigate by headings, which is why the outline matters.

interview.question: What would you check when reviewing an AI-generated form?
interview.answer: Each input has an associated label, appropriate input types and autocomplete attributes, a real submit button inside a form element, visible error messages tied to fields, and server-side validation in addition to any HTML validation.
interview.explanation: Linking client-side semantics to server-side validation shows full-stack awareness.

example.title: Refactoring generated 'div soup' into semantic HTML
example.body: An assistant generated a header built from divs, with a clickable div as the menu button. The refactor uses header, nav, a real button and a list of links. Visual appearance can stay identical through CSS, but keyboard users can now tab to the button, screen readers announce a navigation landmark, and the code explains itself.

practice.title: Check a page's heading outline
practice.statement: Each input line is a heading such as 'h2 Courses'. Print the outline: each heading on its own line as '- <text>' indented by two spaces per level below h1. Then report issues in document order: the first heading is not h1 ('first heading is hN, expected h1'), a heading goes deeper by more than one level compared with the previous heading ('skipped from hA to hB at '<text>''), and every h1 after the first ('extra h1 '<text>''). Print each issue as 'Issue: <message>', then 'Result: OK' or 'Result: <n> issue(s)'.
practice.objective: Apply heading-hierarchy rules by building an outline and reporting structural problems.

takeaways: Choose elements for meaning; style with CSS.
Landmarks (header, nav, main, footer) make pages navigable for assistive technology.
Use one h1 and do not skip heading levels when going deeper.
Use <button> for actions and <a href> for navigation, never clickable divs.
Every input needs a label; every meaningful image needs alt text.
Review AI-generated markup for div soup; it is a common weakness.

samples.title: CSS Layout: Box Model, Flexbox and Grid
samples.definition: CSS layout is how the browser sizes and positions boxes. Every element is a box made of content, padding, border and margin (the box model). Flexbox arranges items along a single axis (a row or a column) and distributes spare space between them, while CSS grid places items into rows and columns at the same time. Together they replace older float- and table-based layouts.
objectives: Explain the CSS box model and why box-sizing: border-box is the common default.
Use flexbox for one-dimensional layouts and explain flex-grow, flex-shrink and flex-basis.
Use CSS grid for two-dimensional layouts with grid-template-columns, fr units and gap.
Choose between flexbox and grid for a given layout.
Compute how flexbox distributes free space between items.

interview.question: Explain the CSS box model.
interview.answer: Every element is a box with content, padding, border and margin. With content-box sizing, width applies to content only and padding and border add to it; with border-box, width includes padding and border.
interview.explanation: Mentioning why teams set border-box globally shows practical experience.

interview.question: When do you use flexbox versus grid?
interview.answer: Flexbox for one-dimensional layouts where content size drives placement, such as navbars and button rows. Grid for two-dimensional layouts where I define rows and columns, such as page shells and galleries. I often nest flexbox inside grid items.
interview.explanation: Giving one concrete example of each is what interviewers look for.

interview.question: How do you centre an element horizontally and vertically?
interview.answer: Make the parent display: flex with justify-content: center and align-items: center, or display: grid with place-items: center.
interview.explanation: Both modern answers are accepted; avoid only quoting old absolute-position hacks.

interview.question: What does flex: 1 mean?
interview.answer: It is shorthand for flex-grow: 1, flex-shrink: 1 and flex-basis: 0%. Because every item starts from zero and grows equally, items with flex: 1 share the space equally regardless of content (subject to their minimum content size).
interview.explanation: Contrast with flex: auto (basis auto), where items start from their content size.

interview.question: An AI-generated layout overflows on small screens. How do you debug it?
interview.answer: Inspect elements in DevTools to find the widest box, check for fixed widths, long unbroken words, images without max-width: 100%, and flex items that cannot shrink below their content (fix with min-width: 0). Then replace fixed widths with flexible units.
interview.explanation: The min-width: 0 detail on flex items is a classic senior-level insight.

example.title: A dashboard shell with grid and a toolbar with flexbox
example.body: The page uses grid areas for the header, sidebar and main region. Inside the header, flexbox pushes the logo left and the actions right. The cards area uses auto-fit and minmax so the number of columns adapts to the screen width.

practice.title: Simulate flexbox space distribution
practice.statement: Given a flex container width, a gap and items with basis, grow and shrink, compute each item's final width (ignore minimum content sizes). free = width - sum(bases) - gap * (items - 1). If free >= 0, each item gets basis + free * grow / totalGrow (items keep their basis when totalGrow is 0). If free < 0, each item gets basis + free * (shrink * basis) / sum(shrink * basis) (items keep their basis when that sum is 0). Print the free space, then each item's width rounded to at most two decimals.
practice.objective: Understand flex-grow and flex-shrink by computing final item widths.

takeaways: Use box-sizing: border-box so width includes padding and border.
Flexbox handles one axis; grid handles rows and columns together.
Free space is shared by flex-grow; overflow is removed by flex-shrink weighted by basis.
flex: 1 means grow 1, shrink 1, basis 0, giving equal widths.
repeat(auto-fit, minmax(...)) creates responsive grids without media queries.
Combine them: grid for the page, flexbox for components.

firstLesson.title: What Vibe Coding Is: Promise, Workflow and Risks
objectives: Define vibe coding and distinguish it from disciplined AI-assisted engineering.
Describe the basic loop: describe, generate, run, inspect, refine.
Explain where vibe coding shines (prototypes, glue code) and where it is dangerous (auth, payments, data).
List the main risks of accepting code you have not read: bugs, security holes, licence and maintenance debt.
Answer interview questions about your personal policy for using AI-generated code.
firstLesson.definition: Vibe coding is a style of building software where you describe what you want in natural language and let an AI assistant write most of the code, judging progress mainly by whether the result runs and looks right. The term was popularised by Andrej Karpathy in early 2025. In professional settings it is a starting point: engineers still own the code, so they read, test and review what the AI produces before it ships.

theory.heading: From autocomplete to describing whole features
theory.body: Early coding assistants completed a line or a function as you typed. Modern assistants can take a paragraph of requirements and produce several files, run commands and fix their own errors. This shifts the developer's job from typing every line to specifying intent, steering the assistant and verifying the result. Vibe coding is the extreme end of this spectrum: you mostly accept what the model writes and react to what you see.
points: Inline completion: suggests the next lines inside the editor.
Chat assistants: answer questions and generate snippets you paste in.
Agentic assistants: edit multiple files, run tests and iterate with less supervision.
The more autonomy the tool has, the more important review and tests become.

theory.heading: The vibe coding loop
theory.body: The workflow is a fast feedback loop. You state a goal, the assistant generates code, you run it, observe what happens and describe the next change or the error. The loop is powerful because each iteration is cheap. It becomes risky when the only check is 'it seems to work', because many defects (security, edge cases, performance) are invisible in a quick manual test.
points: Describe: state the goal, constraints and context.
Generate: let the assistant write or edit code.
Run: execute the app or tests.
Inspect: read the diff and the behaviour, not just the screen.
Refine: give precise feedback or roll back and try again.

theory.heading: Where it works well and where it does not
theory.body: Vibe coding is excellent for throwaway prototypes, internal tools, learning a new library, boilerplate and UI experiments, because the cost of a hidden bug is low and speed matters most. It is a poor fit for authentication, payments, personal data, concurrency and anything regulated, because a subtle mistake can leak data or lose money and the person who accepted the code may not understand it well enough to fix it.
points: Good fit: prototypes, demos, scripts, scaffolding, exploring an unfamiliar API.
Poor fit without careful review: auth, payments, data migrations, security-sensitive logic.
Rule of thumb: the higher the cost of a bug, the more you must read and test.

theory.heading: Risks of accepting unread code
theory.body: Language models predict plausible code; plausible is not the same as correct. Generated code can call functions that do not exist, use outdated APIs, skip input validation, hard-code secrets, add unnecessary dependencies or duplicate logic. Over time a codebase built from unreviewed generations becomes hard to change because nobody holds a mental model of it.
points: Correctness: off-by-one errors, missed edge cases, invented APIs (hallucinations).
Security: injection, missing authorisation checks, exposed keys.
Supply chain: unknown or even non-existent packages suggested by the model.
Maintainability: inconsistent style, duplicated code, no tests.
Ownership: you are accountable for every line you merge, whoever wrote it.

theory.heading: Responsible AI-assisted engineering
theory.body: Teams that use AI well keep the speed and add guardrails: small changes, version control checkpoints, automated tests, linters, code review and security scanning. The engineer acts as an editor and reviewer. Interviewers increasingly ask how you use AI, and the strongest answer shows both productivity and judgement.
points: Work in small, reviewable steps and commit often.
Ask for tests alongside code and run them.
Read every diff; ask the AI to explain anything unclear.
Scale review effort with risk.

example.title: A prototype that works but is not production-ready
example.body: A student asks an assistant: 'Build a page where users sign up with email and password and see a dashboard.' Within minutes the page works in the browser. A review then finds that passwords are stored in plain text in localStorage, there is no server-side check, and the dashboard is visible to anyone who edits a flag in the browser. The demo is fine for a hackathon; shipping it would be a security incident. The fix is to move authentication to a server, hash passwords and check sessions on every request.

use_cases.title: Hackathon prototypes
use_cases.description: Turn an idea into a clickable demo in hours to test whether users care, accepting that the code may be rewritten.

use_cases.title: Internal tools and scripts
use_cases.description: Generate a CSV cleaner or a small admin page where the audience is small and the blast radius of a bug is limited.

use_cases.title: Learning a new framework
use_cases.description: Ask the assistant to scaffold a feature, then read and question the code to learn the framework's patterns.

use_cases.title: Boilerplate in production apps
use_cases.description: Generate forms, types, tests and configuration, with normal code review before merge.

demonstration.description: Compare a 'pure vibe' request with a disciplined one for the same feature. The second prompt states constraints and asks for tests, which makes the output easier to verify.

code.source:
Vibe prompt:
  Make a function that validates Indian phone numbers.

Disciplined prompt:
  Write a JavaScript function isValidIndianMobile(s) that returns true for 10-digit
  numbers starting with 6-9, optionally prefixed by +91 or 0, ignoring spaces.
  Return false for anything else. Include 6 example calls with expected results,
  covering an empty string and a number with letters.

demonstration.output:
Vibe prompt -> a regex that may or may not handle +91, spaces or a leading 0; you cannot tell without testing.
Disciplined prompt -> a function plus explicit cases such as isValidIndianMobile('+91 98765 43210') === true and isValidIndianMobile('12345') === false, which you can run immediately.

The core loop is describe, generate, run, inspect and refine.
It is ideal for prototypes and low-risk code, risky for auth, payments and data.
Plausible code is not proven code: read diffs and run tests.
You own every line you merge, regardless of who or what wrote it.
Scale the amount of review with the cost of a bug.

practice.objective: Turn the idea 'scale review effort with risk' into a simple, explicit scoring rule.
practice.statement: A team receives several AI-generated changes. Each change has a name, a number of changed lines, an area and whether it includes tests. Score each change: area weight ui=1, logic=2, data=3, auth=4, payments=4 (any other area counts as 2). Add 2 if more than 400 lines changed, otherwise add 1 if more than 100 lines changed. Add 2 if the change has no tests. A score of 6 or more is HIGH, 4 or 5 is MEDIUM, anything lower is LOW. practice.input_format: First line: N (number of changes). Next N lines: name|lines|area|tests where tests is yes or no.
practice.output_format: N lines of the form '<name>: <LEVEL> (score <s>)', then one line 'Review first: <name>'.

example.output:
navbar: LOW (score 1)
checkout: HIGH (score 7)
login: MEDIUM (score 4)
report: MEDIUM (score 5)
Review first: checkout

constraints: 1 <= N <= 100; line counts are non-negative integers.
Area and the tests flag are case-insensitive; trim spaces around fields.
The input is a global string named stdin; print with console.log.
explanation: Split the input into lines and read N from the first line.
For each change, split on '|' and trim every field.
Start from the area weight (default 2), then add size and missing-test penalties.
Map the score to HIGH, MEDIUM or LOW with two thresholds.
Track the highest score using a strict '>' so the earliest change wins ties.

quiz.question: Which description best matches vibe coding?
options: Describing intent in natural language and letting AI generate most of the code, judging by results
Pair programming with another human over video
Compiling code without running any tests
Writing every line by hand and using AI only for documentation
quiz.explanation: Vibe coding relies on natural-language intent and AI generation, with progress judged mainly by whether the result works.

quiz.question: Which task is the safest fit for a fast, lightly reviewed vibe-coding approach?
options: A throwaway prototype to show a UI idea to classmates
A database migration on production customer data
Payment refund logic for a live store
Password reset flow for a banking app
quiz.explanation: A throwaway prototype has a low cost of failure. The others can lose money or leak data if a subtle bug slips through.

quiz.question: Why is 'it runs and looks right' an insufficient check for AI-generated code?
options: AI-generated code cannot be version controlled
Many defects such as missing authorisation or edge-case bugs are invisible in a quick manual test
Generated code always fails to compile
Browsers cannot run AI-generated JavaScript
quiz.explanation: Security flaws, edge cases and performance problems often do not show up when you click through the happy path.

quiz.question: A generated signup stores this in the browser. What is the most serious problem?
options: JSON.stringify is slower than string concatenation
localStorage keys must be uppercase
The email should be stored before the password
The password is stored in plain text and login state is a client-side flag anyone can set
quiz.explanation: Plain-text passwords in the browser and a forgeable login flag mean there is no real authentication. Auth must be verified on a server.

quiz.question: Your team wants to keep AI speed but reduce risk. Which practice helps most?
options: Keep changes small, commit often and require tests plus review before merge
Disable linters because AI code has its own style
Let the assistant choose and install any packages it suggests
Accept large multi-file generations in one commit to save time
quiz.explanation: Small reviewable steps with tests and review keep the fast loop while catching mistakes early.
